slides.title: Frame Allocation
slides.body: Frame Allocation

slides.title: Frame Allocation Problem
slides.body:
Sharing Limited Frames
Multiple processes compete for a fixed pool of physical frames
Too few frames per process causes frequent page faults and poor performance
slides.notes: So, this diagram shows the basic memory-allocation challenge: P1 through P6 are all competing for the same fixed pool of physical frames. The OS has to divide these limited frames among the active processes, and if a process receives too few, it will repeatedly need pages that are not currently in memory, causing frequent page faults and poor performance.

slides.title: Frame Allocation Problem
slides.body:
Sharing Limited Frames
Total frames are fixed by physical memory size
01
02
03
Frames must be split across all active processes
Too few frames per process raises fault rate
slides.notes: Now, the key challenge is deciding how to distribute memory efficiently. The number of available frames is limited by the physical memory, so the OS cannot create additional frames when more processes arrive. These frames have to be shared among all active processes, and if a process receives too little memory, it may experience frequent page faults and perform poorly.

slides.title: Frame Allocation Problem
slides.body:
Sharing Limited Frames
Three schemes address this:
slides.notes: let’s look at the three common ways the operating system can distribute these limited frames.

slides.title: Frame Allocation Problem
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A hostel warden splitting a fixed number of rooms among many students — just as the operating system splits fixed frames among competing processes.

slides.title: Minimum Frame Requirement
slides.body:
Instruction Frame Needs
Every process needs a minimum frame count to execute even one instruction without repeated faults, fixed by the instruction set architecture
slides.notes: So, a process cannot run with just any number of frames. It needs enough memory to fetch and execute an instruction properly, and that minimum is determined by the architecture of the system.

slides.title: Minimum Frame Requirement
slides.body:
Instruction Frame Needs
One instruction may touch several pages at once
01
02
03
Indirect addressing can chain through pointer pages
Minimum frame count depends on architecture design
slides.notes: Now, an instruction may need to access more than one page, especially when indirect addressing involves additional pointer pages. So, the minimum number of frames required depends on how the system's architecture handles these memory accesses.

slides.title: Equal Allocation Scheme
slides.body:
Same Frames Each
Equal allocation splits total frames evenly across all processes, regardless of process size or need
slides.notes: Moving on, equal allocation simply treats every process the same. In the diagram, the available frames are divided evenly among P1, P2, P3, and P4, so each process receives the same number of frames, even if their actual memory requirements are different. It is simple to implement, but a larger process |may not get enough frames while a smaller one may receive more than it needs.

slides.title: Equal Allocation Scheme
slides.body:
Same Frames Each
Frames per process equals total frames divided by count
01
02
03
Simple to implement and easy to reason about
Ignores actual size differences between processes
slides.notes: So, in equal allocation, we simply divide the available frames equally among all processes. For example, with 90 frames and 3 processes, each process gets 30 frames. It’s straightforward to implement, but the drawback is that it treats all processes the same, even when their memory requirements are different.

slides.title: Proportional Allocation Scheme
slides.body:
Size-Based Frame Share
Proportional allocation gives each process frames proportional to its size, so larger processes receive more frames than smaller ones
slides.notes: Now, proportional allocation adjusts the split according to process size. In the diagram, P1 is the largest, so it receives the most frames, P2 receives fewer, and the smaller P3 gets the least. The idea is to use the limited frames more fairly by giving a larger share to processes that have greater memory requirements.

slides.title: Proportional Allocation Scheme
slides.body:
ai = (si ÷ S) × m → ai is the number of frames allocated to process i
01
02
03
si is the size of process i in pages
S is the sum of sizes of all processes
04
m is the total number of available frames
Assume total available frames (m) = 62
Size-Based Frame Share
slides.notes: Moving on, proportional allocation gives each process a share of the available frames based on its size. Here, si is the size of process i in pages, S is the combined size of all processes, and m is the total number of available frames, which is 62. So, we divide si by S to find that process's share, and multiply it by m to get the actual frames allocated, represented by ai.

slides.title: Proportional Allocation Scheme
slides.body: Size-Based Frame Share
slides.notes: Now, let’s apply the formula to these two processes. Since P2 is much larger than P1, it receives a much larger share of the 62 available frames. This gives P1 approximately 4.53 frames and P2 approximately 57.47 frames, showing how proportional allocation adjusts the memory share according to process size.

slides.title: Proportional Allocation Scheme
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes:
Grain rationed to families in proportion to family size —
 just as proportional allocation gives each process frames in proportion to its size.

slides.title: Priority Allocation Scheme
slides.body:
Importance-Based Frames
Priority allocation uses process importance, not just size, to decide frame share; higher-priority processes receive more frames
Priority: High
Priority: Low

slides.title: Priority Allocation Scheme
slides.body:
Importance-Based Frames
01
High-priority or interactive processes get more frames
02
Low-priority processes may receive fewer frames and experience a higher page-fault rate
03
Priority allocation can be combined with process size or other factors in some systems
slides.notes:
Next, frame allocation can also depend on how important a process is. For example, an interactive or high-priority process needs quick responses, so giving it more frames helps reduce page faults and improves responsiveness. A low-priority process may receive fewer frames, 
which can lead to a higher page-fault rate. In some systems, priority is not used alone; the OS can combine it with the process size or other factors to decide the final allocation.

slides.title: Priority Allocation Scheme
slides.body: Importance-Based Frames

slides.title: Priority Allocation Scheme
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A hospital gives ICU beds to the most critical patients first, not equally to every ward — just as priority allocation gives more frames to higher-priority processes.

slides.title: Replacement Scope
slides.body: Replacement Scope
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Replacement Scope

slides.title: Replacement Scope
slides.body:
Whose Frames Change
On a page fault, the OS must pick a victim frame. Scope decides which processes' frames are eligible for that choice
Victim frame
slides.notes: Moving on, when a page fault occurs, the OS has to choose a frame to replace. In the diagram, the OS selects the highlighted frame as the victim frame, which means the page currently occupying that frame will be removed and replaced with the required page. The replacement scope determines which processes' frames the OS is allowed to consider for this selection.

slides.title: Replacement Scope
slides.body:
Whose Frames Change
Victim frame chosen by a replacement algorithm
01
02
03
Scope defines the eligible frame pool
Two policies exist: global and local
slides.notes: Now, whenever a page fault occurs, the replacement algorithm decides which frame should be removed, called the victim frame. The replacement scope determines the set of frames from which that victim can be selected. Based on this scope, we have two approaches: global replacement and local replacement.

slides.title: Global Replacement
slides.body:
Any Frame Eligible
A faulting process may select a victim frame from any process in the system, not only from its own frames.
Victim frame
slides.notes: Next, in global replacement, the OS is not restricted to the frames of the process that caused the page fault. In the diagram, P2 has the fault, but the highlighted victim frame can be selected from the available frames of the system, including frames belonging to other processes such as P1. This gives the OS greater flexibility in using memory.

slides.title: Global Replacement
slides.body:
Any Frame Eligible
Faulting process can take another process's frame
01
02
03
Frame counts per process vary over time
May increase page faults in other processes by taking their frames
slides.notes: Now, the flexibility of global replacement also means one process can take a frame that was previously assigned to another process. Because of this, the number of frames available to each process can keep changing over time. The benefit is better overall flexibility, but taking frames from one process can also increase its page faults and affect its performance.

slides.title: Local Replacement
slides.body:
Own Frames Only
A faulting process selects its victim frame only from among its own currently allocated frames.
Victim frame
Faulting Process
slides.notes: Moving on, local replacement keeps the memory decision within the faulting process itself. In the diagram, the faulting process has several allocated frames, and the highlighted victim frame is selected from those frames only. So, unlike global replacement, the process cannot take a frame belonging to another process.

slides.title: Local Replacement
slides.body:
Own Frames Only
Faulting process replaces only its own page
01
02
03
Frame count per process stays fixed
Isolates one process's faults from others
slides.notes: Next, with local replacement, a process handles its own page faults using only the frames already assigned to it. So its frame allocation remains fixed, and one process's page-fault activity does not take frames away from other processes.

slides.body: Trade-offs Compared
tables: May improve by adapting to changing needs

slides.title: Thrashing
slides.body: Thrashing
slides.notes: Next we will learn about the Thrashing,

slides.title: What Is Thrashing
slides.body:
Paging Dominates Execution
Frames allocated fall below active page need
01
02
03
A large proportion of referenced pages cause page faults
CPU utilization collapses despite busy processes
Thrashing occurs when a process spends more time paging than executing, because it holds fewer frames than its actual need
slides.notes: Now, imagine a process has fewer frames than the pages it actively needs, so the pages it needs keep getting pushed out of memory and loaded back again. As a result, the system spends most of its time handling page faults instead of actually executing processes. This is called thrashing, and when it becomes severe, CPU utilization can drop dramatically even though the processes are active.

slides.title: What Is Thrashing
slides.body:
Paging Dominates Execution
Optimal
Thrashing
Improving Throughput
Degree of Multiprogramming
CPU Utilization
slides.notes: Moving on, this graph shows why adding more processes does not always improve performance. Initially, increasing the degree of multiprogramming keeps more work available and improves CPU utilization. At the optimal point, utilization is highest. Beyond that, memory pressure increases, page faults become frequent, and the system enters thrashing, causing CPU utilization to fall.

slides.title: What Is Thrashing
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A student has only one book on the desk, but needs many books to study. They keep getting up to bring another book and spend more time fetching books than studying — just as a process spends more time loading pages than executing.

slides.title: How Thrashing Begins
slides.body:
Vicious Fault Cycle
Thrashing builds as a self-reinforcing cycle: 
Faults grow
CPU idles
Worsening the fault rate
Degree of multiprogramming increases
slides.notes: Next, thrashing creates a cycle where the problem keeps getting worse. As page faults increase, the CPU spends more time waiting for pages instead of executing processes. This leads to low CPU utilization, and the system may respond by adding more processes, which means fewer frames are available for each process. That causes even more page faults and makes the situation worse.

slides.title: How Thrashing Begins
slides.body:
Vicious Fault Cycle
Low frames per process raise fault frequency
01
02
03
Faulting process queues for the paging device
CPU sits idle waiting for pages to load
04
05
Low CPU use triggers scheduler to add processes
More processes shrink frames per process further
slides.notes: Next, the cycle starts when a process has too few frames, causing frequent page faults and forcing it to wait for the paging device to bring pages into memory. While processes are waiting, the CPU remains underutilized, so the scheduler may admit more processes. These additional processes compete for the same frames, reducing the frames available to each process even further and causing more faults.

slides.title: How Thrashing Begins
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes: A highway is already crowded, but more cars are allowed onto it because some lanes look unused, making the traffic jam worse — just as adding processes when CPU utilization is low can worsen thrashing.

slides.title: CPU Utilization Collapse
slides.body:
Multiprogramming Vs Utilization
CPU utilization rises with multiprogramming degree up to an optimal point, then collapses sharply once thrashing sets in.
slides.notes: Now, the relationship is straightforward: with a low degree of multiprogramming, frames are plentiful, so there are fewer faults but the CPU may remain underused. As we add processes, we reach an optimal point where enough frames are available and CPU utilization is highest. Beyond that, frames become scarce, page faults dominate, and thrashing causes CPU utilization to crash.
tables: Frames plentiful, few faults, CPU underused
Frames scarce, faults dominate, utilization crashes

slides.title: Locality & Working Set
slides.body: Locality & Working Set
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Locality & Working Set

slides.title: Locality Model
slides.body:
Clustered Page References
A process does not reference all its pages uniformly. At any point, execution stays within a small, shifting set of pages called a locality
Page 1
Page 2
Page 3
Page 4
.
.
.
Locality
slides.notes: Moving on, a process usually does not need all of its pages at the same time. During a particular phase of execution, it tends to repeatedly access a small group of nearby pages. In the diagram, the process is currently working mainly with Page 2 and Page 3; this frequently accessed group is called a locality. As execution progresses, the locality can shift to another set of pages.

slides.title: Locality Model
slides.body:
Clustered Page References
Execution moves through distinct phases over time
01
02
03
Each phase references its own small page set
Localities shift as the process progresses
04
Explains why few frames can still work
slides.notes: Now, a process typically works in phases rather than accessing all its pages randomly. During each phase, it repeatedly uses a small set of pages, and as the process moves to another phase, that set changes. This explains why a process can perform well with relatively few frames, as long as those frames cover its current locality.

slides.title: Working Set Model
slides.body:
Recent Reference Window
The working set formalises locality: 
It is the set of pages referenced in the most recent window of references
Approximating the process's current locality
slides.notes: Moving on, the working set gives us a practical way to identify a process's current locality. We look at the pages it has referenced within a recent window of memory references; those pages together form the working set, which gives us an estimate of what the process currently needs in memory.

slides.title: Working Set Model
slides.body:
Recent Reference Window
WS(t, Δ) = pages referenced in last Δ references
01
02
03
Δ is the working-set window size
WSS = |WS(t, Δ)| is the working set size
04
WSS approximates frames the process needs now
slides.notes: Next, we can represent the working set more precisely. WS(t, Δ) means the distinct pages referenced during the most recent Δ references, where Δ is the size of our reference window. The number of pages in that set, written as WSS = |WS(t, Δ)|, estimates how many frames the process currently needs to run efficiently.

slides.title: Choosing Window Size
slides.body:
Delta Sizing Trade-off
The window size Δ controls how accurately the working set tracks true locality; picking it wrong distorts the estimate in opposite ways.
slides.notes: Moving on, the choice of Δ, or window size, affects how accurately the working set represents the process's current locality. If Δ is too small, some needed pages may be missed; if it is too large, pages from different localities may get included together. So, a well-chosen Δ gives a closer picture of the pages the process currently needs.

slides.title: Working Set Demand
slides.body:
Total Demand D
Summing every process's working set size gives the system's total frame demand, which the operating system compares against available frames
Working set 1
Working set 2
Working set 3
slides.notes: Now, we can estimate the total memory demand of the system by adding the working-set sizes of all active processes. In the diagram, the working sets of P1, P2, and P3 are combined to get the total demand, which the OS then compares with the number of frames actually available.

slides.title: Working Set Demand
slides.body:
Total Demand D
D = sum of WSSi over all processes
01
02
03
m is the total number of available frames
If D > m, the system may experience thrashing
04
OS should keep D ≤ m
slides.notes: Next, we calculate the system's total frame demand by adding the working-set size of every process, which gives us D. Here, WSSᵢ represents the working-set size of process i, while m is the total number of available frames. If D becomes greater than m, there aren't enough frames to satisfy the processes' current needs, increasing the risk of thrashing. So, the OS should try to maintain D ≤ m.

slides.title: Working Set Example
slides.body:
Computing WSS Numerically
A short reference string with a chosen window Δ shows how the working set and its size are computed at a given time t
slides.notes: Now, let’s see how the working set is obtained from an actual reference string. At t = 10, we look at the most recent 4 references, because Δ is 4. These references are 7, 7, 5, and 1; since we count distinct pages only, the working set becomes {1, 5, 7}, giving a WSS of 3.

slides.title: Controlling Thrashing
slides.body: Controlling Thrashing
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Controlling Thrashing

slides.title: Need For Control
slides.body:
Before Collapse Occurs
Working sets reveal when demand exceeds frames, but the operating system still needs a live mechanism to act before utilisation collapses
Operating systems
slides.notes: Moving on, the working set helps us identify when memory demand is becoming too high, but simply detecting the problem is not enough. The OS needs a mechanism that can respond before the system reaches severe thrashing and CPU utilization collapses.

slides.title: Need For Control
slides.body:
Before Collapse Occurs
Detection must happen while faults are rising
01
02
03
Static allocation alone cannot react in time
Control means adjusting frames or process count
Two approaches follow: the Page-Fault Frequency (PFF) scheme, and a set of general prevention techniques
slides.notes: Next, the OS needs to detect the problem while page faults are still increasing, rather than waiting for CPU utilization to collapse. A fixed allocation cannot respond quickly to changing memory needs, so the OS may need to adjust frame allocation or control the number of active processes. Two approaches help with this: Page-Fault Frequency (PFF) and other general thrashing prevention techniques.

slides.title: PFF Scheme Concept
slides.body:
Upper Lower Bounds
The page-fault frequency scheme directly monitors each process's fault rate and compares it against a defined upper and lower bound
Page-Fault Frequency
slides.notes: Moving on, the Page-Fault Frequency scheme keeps track of how often each process is experiencing page faults. In the diagram, P1, P2, and P3 each have their own fault rate, and the OS compares these rates with a predefined upper and lower bound to decide whether a process needs more or fewer frames.

slides.title: PFF Scheme Concept
slides.body:
Upper, Lower Bounds
Fault rate above upper bound signals too few frames
01
02
03
Fault rate below lower bound signals excess frames
Bounds define an acceptable fault-rate band
slides.notes: Next, the OS uses these two bounds to judge whether a process has enough memory. If its fault rate goes above the upper bound, it likely needs more frames. If it falls below the lower bound, the process may have more frames than necessary, so some can be taken back. Together, the bounds create an acceptable range of page-fault frequency.

slides.title: PFF Scheme Concept
slides.body:
Upper, Lower Bounds
Upper Bound
Number of frames
Page fault rate
Lower Bound
Increase number of frames
Decrease number of frames
slides.notes: Now, this graph shows how the OS uses the fault rate to adjust frame allocation. When the fault rate is above the upper bound, the process is experiencing too many faults, so the OS should increase its frames. When the rate falls below the lower bound, the process has more frames than it needs, so the OS can decrease the allocation. Between these two bounds, the fault rate is considered acceptable.

slides.title: PFF Control Actions
slides.body:
Adjusting Frame Counts
Crossing a bound triggers a concrete action: frames are added, removed, or a process is suspended when none remain free.
slides.notes: Moving on, once the fault rate crosses a bound, the OS takes a specific action. If it goes above the upper bound, more frames are allocated to the process. If there are no free frames, the OS may suspend a low-priority process to free memory. On the other hand, if the rate falls below the lower bound, excess frames can be taken back from that process.

slides.title: Preventing Thrashing
slides.body:
Key Techniques List
Beyond PFF, several complementary techniques keep total frame demand within the available supply and avoid the fault-idle cycle
slides.notes: Next, PFF is one way to control thrashing, but it is not the only option. The OS can use other techniques to keep the total memory demand within the available frames and prevent the system from getting trapped in a cycle of continuous page faults and CPU idle time.

slides.title: Preventing Thrashing
slides.body:
Key Techniques List
Limit degree of multiprogramming admitted at once
01
02
03
Use local replacement to contain a process's faults
Suspend or swap out processes under memory pressure
04
Monitor working set or fault rate continuously
slides.notes: Now, the main goal is to make sure processes are not competing for more memory than the system can provide. One way is to keep the number of active processes under control; another is to isolate memory pressure using local replacement. If memory becomes heavily constrained, some processes can be temporarily suspended or swapped out. Meanwhile, monitoring the working set or fault rate helps the OS recognize increasing pressure early and take action before thrashing begins.

slides.title: Thrashing Control Today
slides.body:
Modern Practice Notes
Large modern RAM sizes make severe thrashing rarer, but virtual memory managers still track fault rates and cap process counts under memory pressure.
slides.notes: Finally, severe thrashing is less common today because modern systems generally have much more physical memory. However, virtual memory managers still need to watch page-fault behavior and may limit the number of active processes when memory pressure becomes high, preventing the system from falling into the same fault-heavy cycle.

slides.title: Thrashing Control Today
slides.body:
Modern Practice Notes
Cloud VMs and containers still enforce memory limits
01
02
03
Hypervisors monitor guest fault rates similarly
Core concepts remain standard interview fundamentals
slides.notes: Finally, these ideas also apply to modern environments. Cloud VMs and containers still have memory limits, so excessive memory demand can lead to pressure and performance issues. Similarly, hypervisors monitor memory and fault behavior across guest systems. So, although the technology has evolved, the core ideas of frame allocation, page faults, and thrashing remain important OS fundamentals and common interview concepts.
